text:
Courgettes and Marrows.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Courgettes and marrows are the same crop at different stages: courgettes are picked young, firm and tender; marrows grow larger for fresh use or storage. Modern courgette varieties keep producing small fruits, often several each week in summer warmth. Total yield depends on season and picking.

Quick facts
Sow indoors

Late Apr–May in warm pots.

Harvest

Jul – Oct

Germination

5–8 days

Sowing depth

Indoors: 5/8 in.; direct outdoors: 1 in.

Sow

Late May–Jun in warm soil.

Plant out

Mid-May–Jun, after frost.

Row spacing

Each way, at least: bush types 3 ft; trailing marrows 5 ft.

Yield per plant

About 4 mature marrows; courgettes: several young fruits weekly at peak.

Plant spacing

one plant per prepared pocket or station

Ready in

About 8–14 weeks from sowing; pick courgettes young

Recommended varieties
COURGETTE
Defender F1

A productive green courgette with useful virus resistance for repeat summer picking.

COURGETTE
Early Gem F1

An early green courgette. Pick young and often for continued summer crops.

COURGETTE
Parador F1

Easy-to-spot yellow fruits add colour alongside green varieties.

COURGETTE
Astia F1

Compact plants for containers or small beds; pick young and often.

MARROW
Tiger Cross F1

A dark-green, pale-striped marrow. Grow larger for stuffing while maintaining regular harvests.

Key risks
Slugs

Slugs chew seedlings, especially in cold, wet weather.

Mildew

White powder coats leaves, often late in the season.

Poor pollination

If fruitlets yellow, wither or fail to swell, pollination may be poor.

Fruit rot

Fruit resting on wet soil may soften and rot.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
46
FRUITING CROPS

Warmth and moisture drive growth.

Plant after frost and avoid cold, wet starts or drought checks.

Pick courgettes frequently.

Young tender fruits keep plants cropping; mature marrows are a different use.

Soil & preparation
Use a warm, sunny, sheltered site with rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil. Prepare compost-rich planting pockets.
Mulch generously and leave enough room for the chosen bush or trailing type. Avoid poorly drained ground.
Sowing & planting
Sow on edge
Keep one strong plant
Sow in pots 

Set one seed on edge in each pot or module. Keep warm and lightly moist. Cold, wet compost can rot the seed.

Plant out 

Harden off and plant one per pocket after frost. Give trailing marrows their wider spacing. Use fleece temporarily if nights turn cool.

Sow outside 

In warm soil, sow two or three seeds at each pocket. Keep the strongest seedling.

Looking after the crop
Water at the roots in dry weather and as fruits swell. Mulch with compost. Keep the foliage dry where possible.
Let insects reach the flowers. If fruit fails to set, transfer pollen from a male flower to the centre of a female flower, recognisable by the tiny fruit behind it.
Use strong supports for trailing marrows, tying stems gently. Support heavy fruit separately; restrict unwanted extension if needed.
Harvesting & storage
Cut young courgettes, often 4–6 in. long, daily or every other day in warmth. Leave a short stem; do not snap off. Remove misshapen first fruits promptly. Overgrown fruit slows further cropping.
Pick marrows tender for immediate use, or let selected storage fruits develop hard skins before frost. Handle gently and keep dry.
Discard unusually bitter fruit. Wear gloves or long sleeves if stems irritate your skin; flowers can also be used in the kitchen.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Slugs	Young plants are chewed.	Protect establishment; inspect and hand-pick in damp weather.
Mildew	White powder on older leaves.	Keep roots moist; remove badly affected leaves as needed.
Poor pollination	Fruitlets yellow or fail to swell.	Let insects in. Hand-pollinate if needed.
Fruit rot	Fruit softens where it touches wet ground.	Lift onto a clean support; remove rotten fruit.
Cucumber mosaic virus	Mottled, puckered leaves; stunted growth.	Remove infected plants; clear weed hosts and monitor aphids.
Bitterness	Fruit tastes unusually bitter.	Discard bitter fruit; do not try to make it safe by cooking.
Root rot	Wilting; dark, decaying roots.	Remove collapsed plants; improve drainage and avoid cold wet roots.
Final tips

Raise developing marrows on a clean tile or board to keep their skins dry and sound.

After frost, compost healthy plants; remove virus-infected or badly rotted remains without spreading them.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
See also: Vegetable Troubles 117–121 · Growing Techniques 150
47
FRUITING CROPS
